newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Richardson speaks of Mobutu aides in new government.
newsitem.headline: Richardson speaks of Mobutu aides in new government.

text.p: Acknowledging that rebel leader Laurent Kabila will head any new Zairean government, U.S. envoy Bill Richardson suggested President Mobutu Sese Seko's followers be included in a transition phase.
He said Kabila would "most likely" head a transition government because he has "the guns and has the strength" but that a new government should include all factions.

"The big issue is going to be how much of Mobutu's people, if any at all, are part of that," he said referring to a transition government mediators want Kabila to establish after his all-but-certain takeover of the capital, Kinshasa.

He revealed that the letter he delivered from U.S. President Bill Clinton to Mobutu last weekend said, in effect, "You must engage in face-to-face talks. Eventually it is going to mean there will be a peaceful transition in Zaire with an inclusive government and you should be part of it."

Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, late on Friday conducted a round of television interviews on his shuttle diplomacy in Central Africa. One was with public television's Newshour with Jim Lehrer, another was on the Charlie Rose show on the same network.

He said he was still hopeful of a peaceful transition. He also said he expected a second meeting between Mobutu and Kabila to be held in the Congo next week, although reports from Zaire indicate it may again on a South African ship.
He said Mobutu, who wanted to leave office "gracefully," would nevertheless return to Kinshasa to clear up his affairs after his meeting in Gabon with African leaders.

And he warned Kabila, whom he called "street smart" and pragmatic" but unused to governing, to observe human rights, to allow investigations into massacres and to behave responsibly or forfeit international respect and aid.

"I believe that Mobutu will return to Kinshasa before he heads for the Congo. I believe he is putting his affairs in order. But eventually I do believe there's still a good chance of a peaceful inclusive transition government," he said.

Giving his impressions of Mobutu, Richardson said, the ailing leader, in power for 32 years, needed constant treatment for his prostrate cancer. "He could barely stand up. But he was very mentally alert,"
"But Zaire is too important for there to be a personality cult. Zaire is literally falling apart," he added.

"Our relations with Mobutu have not been that strong," he said. "But nobody had said to him, 'perhaps it is time for you to retire from the political scene.'" He said the president had been told by his advisers that "he could still hang on."
"Unfortunately I was the bearer of a lot of bad news but nonetheless, I believe that Mobutu is now realistic. He is a dignified person. He wants to go out gracefully."
"He is bitter at the United States and some of its other allies for not backing him but the reality is that he's lost support in Kinshasa and throughout the country," he said.

Asked by Rose about money Mobutu is said to have taken out of the country, Richardson said this issue would be "very important for Kabila and difficult to negotiate" as the rebel leader wanted all funds invested in Zaire.

As for Kabila, Richardson called him "very street smart" and "pragmatic" but said he has never governed, "never run anything." Kabila believes "Look, right now I've got the guns. Get Mobutu out and then we can talk," Richardson said.
"And what we are saying to him is that Mobutu probably will leave one way another..but what you need to do is negotiate a transition peacefully."

Richardson warned Kabila that he needed to make sure his troops stopped mistreating Rwandan refugees and punished those responsible for refugee massacres in eastern Zaire if he wanted respect from the international community.
"He is going to need private investment and international assistance to survive, because literally Zaire right at this moment is falling apart," Richardson said.
But without waiting for a peace agreement, American, Canadian and other other Western companies have been making deals with Kabila for mining rights in the areas he controls.
